headline: Ni is from Middle Chinese 二 (nyijH, “two”).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 二 (nyijᴴ, “two”). Compare modern Northern Min 二 (nī).

headline: Tobu is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *tənpu.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *tənpu. Cognate with Okinawan 飛ぶん (tubun).

headline: Hen is from Middle Chinese 變 (MC pjenH).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 變 (MC pjenH).

headline: Naru is possibly a verbalization of na-, the bound form of 音 (ne, “sound”).

sources.quote: Inherited from Old Japanese. Possibly a verbalization of na-, the 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 音(ね) (ne, “sound”).

headline: Oyogu was possibly oyoku, but Ryūkyūan cognates support a voiced g at the end.

sources.quote: Likely from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oyonku. Included in The Tale of Genji from the late 900s or early 1000s. Listed in sources with a note that this may have been pronounced originally as oyoku, however, cognates among the Ryūkyūan languages would seem to support a voiced /ɡ/ as the final consonant. Compare Kunigami 泳じゅん (uijun), Okinawan 泳じゅん (qwiijun).

headline: Yasumi is the stem form of the verb 休む (yasumu, “to rest”).

sources.quote: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 休(やす)む (yasumu, “to rest”).

headline: Fueru is from the Classical Japanese verb 増ゆ (fuyu).

sources.quote: From the Classical Japanese verb 増ゆ (fuyu).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Itasu is the transitive/causative counterpart to the intransitive verb 至る (itaru).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Derived as the transitive/causative counterpart to intransitive verb 至る (itaru, “to come; to go; to reach a point in time or space; to result in”), originally meaning the same as causative conjugation 至らせる (itaraseru, “to make something or someone come or go; to make something reach a point in time or space; to cause a certain result”).

headline: Uru is Old Japanese, and possibly cognate with 得る (eru, “to obtain”), from getting money for the item sold.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Attested in 正倉院文書 (Shōsōin Monjo, “Shōsōin Documents”) with the spelling 宇利 (⟨uri⟩) (Omodaka 1967, p. 136). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *ur-.
Possibly cognate with Old Japanese 得 (u), modern Japanese 得る (eru, “to obtain, to get”), from the sense of getting money in exchange for the item sold.

headline: Itai was itasi in Old Japanese, and might originally have been an interjection like English ouch.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 痛し (itasi), from Proto-Japonic *ita (“painful”). Might originally be an interjection; compare English ouch.

headline: Iro was first attested in the Nihon Shoki meaning “color”, with the romance senses appearing from the 900s.

sources.quote: ⟨iro₂⟩ → */irə/ → /iro/
From Old Japanese.

First attested in the Nihon Shoki with the meaning of color. Senses referring to a person's emotions also appear quite early on. The romance or sex senses appear from the 900s, apparently an influence from Chinese usage, and roughly comparable to the euphemistic usage of English colorful.

headline: Niku is from Middle Chinese 肉 (MC nyuwk).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 肉 (MC nyuwk). Compare modern Hokkien 肉 (jio̍k / lio̍k), Teochew 肉 (ne̍k), or Hakka 肉 (ngiuk⁷).

meaning: to be heard, to be audible
headline: Kikoeru is from 聞こゆ (kikoyu), built on kika, the irrealis of 聞く (kiku, “to hear”), plus ゆ (-yu).

sources.quote: ⟨ki₁ka yu⟩ → ⟨ki₁ko₂yu⟩ → */kʲikəju/ → /kikoju/ → /kikojeru/ → /kikoeru/
From Old Japanese verb 聞こゆ (kikoyu), itself derived from the 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of 聞く (kiku, “to hear, listen”) kika + ゆ (-yu, attributive suffix).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Hajimaru is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pansimara, “to begin”, intransitive.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pansimara (“to begin”, intransitive).

meaning: to get off (a vehicle); to go down, to descend
headline: Oriru is from the classical upper bigrade verb 降る (oru).

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb (ラ行上二段活用) 降(お)る (oru).

headline: Ikiru is from the classical upper bigrade verb 生く.

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb (カ行上二段活用) 生く.

headline: Fuku “clothes” is from Middle Chinese 服 (MC bjuwk).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 服 (MC bjuwk).

headline: Ōkina is the na-adjective form of 大きい, appearing from the Muromachi period.

sources.quote: /opoki/ → /oɸoki/ → /oɸoki na/ → /owoki na/ → /oːki na/
Appears starting from the Muromachi period (室(むろ)町(まち)時(じ)代(だい) (Muromachi jidai), c. 1336–1573).
Derived as the -na adjective construction of -i adjective 大(おお)きい (ōkii, “big, great”), which see for more.

headline: Hashi is tentatively traced to Proto-Japonic *pasui, and probably related to 挟む (hasamu, “to pinch”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, tentatively traced to Proto-Japonic *pasui (compare Ainu パスイ (pasui)). Probably related to 挟む (hasamu, “to pinch, to scissor, to hold between”), possibly also related to 嘴 (“beak”, pitch accent hàshí) or 端 (“tip”, pitch accent háꜜshì).

headline: Me is probably cognate with 見る (miru, “to see”), and may also be cognate with 芽 (me, “bud, shoot”).

sources.quote: ⟨me₂⟩ → */məɨ/ → /me/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mai. Cognate with 目(ま) (ma, bound form). Now the modern Japanese term for eye.
Probably cognate with 見(み)る (miru, “to see, to look”).

May also be cognate with 芽(め) (me, “bud, shoot”), perhaps from the “visually prominent feature” sense, and with suppositional / volitional verb suffix む (mu) (presenting in modern Japanese verb conjugations as the -ō or -yō endings), perhaps from the “seem like, look like” sense.

headline: Dare was tare until around the Edo period, voiced by analogy with 何れ (dore) and 何処 (doko).

sources.quote: /tare/ → /dare/
From earlier tare.

The dare form appears from around the Edo period. The voicing of the initial /t-/ to /d-/ is likely by analogy with other interrogative demonstratives 何れ (dore, “which one”), 何処 (doko, “where”). See etymology 2
Now the primary form, replacing earlier tare.

headline: Owari is the stem form of the verb 終わる (owaru, “to end”).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 終(お)わる (owaru, “to end”, intransitive).

meaning: It's ok (all right); No need to worry; Everything is under control
headline: Daijōbu is from Chinese 大丈夫, equivalent to 大 (dai-) plus 丈夫 (jōbu).

sources.quote: From Chinese 大丈夫, equivalent to 大(だい) (dai-) + 丈(じょう)夫(ぶ) (jōbu).

headline: Yūmei is likely from Middle Chinese 有名, literally “to have + name”.

sources.quote: Likely from Middle Chinese compound 有名 (hjuw^X mjeng, literally “to have + name”). Compare modern Mandarin reading yǒumíng.

headline: Tsukamaeru is possibly 掴ま (tsukama, “to grab”) plus ふ (fu, frequentative suffix).

sources.quote: Possibly from 掴(つか)ま (tsukama, “to grab”, irrealis stem) + ふ (fu, frequentative suffix).

headline: Mimi is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, from Proto-Japonic *mimi.

sources.quote: * ⟨mi₁mi₁⟩ → */mimi/ → /mimi/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *mimi.

headline: Dōbutsuen is 動物 (dōbutsu, “animal”) plus 園 (-en, “garden”).

sources.quote: From 動(どう)物(ぶつ) (dōbutsu, “animal”) + 園(えん) (-en, “garden”).

headline: Kimaru is the intransitive form of the Old Japanese verb 決む (kimu, “to decide”).

sources.quote: Derived as the intransitive form of Old Japanese verb 決(き)む (kimu, “to decide, to conclude; to be decided, to be concluded”).

The source verb kimu appears to follow a common pattern in Old Japanese verbs where the bare form is either transitive or intransitive, depending on context. This pattern persists in some modern verbs, such as つく (tsuku). Many of these Old Japanese verbs developed explicit transitive and intransitive forms, with one group adopting an -aru on the end for the intransitive (as the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis stem”) ending in -a + the conjugating る (ru) as the basic spontaneous or passive verb ending), and an -eru on the end for the transitive (as the 已(い)然(ぜん)形(けい) (izenkei, “realis or potential stem”) + the disappearing る (ru) as a generic verb ending).

headline: Kawaku is cognate with 渇く (kawaku, “to be thirsty”).

sources.quote: Cognate with 渇(かわ)く (kawaku, “to be thirsty”).
